title: Checkpoint: Newer Faiths and America
objective: After this level you can explain how new faiths arise and how America's religious freedom shaped its many churches and communities.
summary: From Virginia's 1786 statute to the 1965 immigration law, new faiths arose from revelations and revivals, and America's religion clauses left room for many churches and communities.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 finale: new faiths keep arising, and some were born in America.
cards.body: From Shiraz to Jamaica to upstate New York, you've met faiths born in modern times. Line them up, then look for the pattern.

cards.headline: How new faiths take root
cards.body: Many new faiths begin with a founder's revelation or a revival: Baha'u'llah's declaration, Joseph Smith's vision, the Azusa Street revival. Others grow out of older traditions: the Latter-day Saints, for example, emerged from the revivals of early 1800s America. In the United States no official church stood in their way: the Establishment Clause bars one, and the Free Exercise Clause protects practice. Since 1965, immigration has added mosques, temples and gurdwaras to the map, while Christians remain the majority.
